Section I: Overarching Principles Section

Chapter 1: Preliminary
      Introduction to the Handbook

1.1   The Handbook is made under section 399 of the SFO and establishes codes or
      guidelines for the authorization of products covered by the Handbook and their offering
      documents and advertisements. These guidelines are not intended to be exhaustive.

1.2   Section I of the Handbook sets out the high-level principles and requirements that are
      intended to apply to all products. More detailed product-specific requirements applicable
      to specific types of products are contained in the applicable product code.

1.3   The Handbook provides general guidelines for authorization of products specifically
      stated in the applicable product codes. The Commission will have regard to both the
      spirit as well as the letter of the General Principles set out in Chapter 3 of this
      Overarching Principles Section in considering products authorization applications and
      whether products should remain authorized.

1.4   All products, their Product Providers and the Specified Entities are expected to comply
      with all applicable principles and requirements set out in Section I of the Handbook in
      addition to the detailed product-specific requirements applicable to specific types of
      products that are contained in the applicable product code.

1.5   The Handbook does not have the force of law and shall not be interpreted in a way that
      will override the provision of any law.

      Effect of breach of the Handbook

1.6   Failure by any person to comply with any applicable provision of the Handbook:

      (a)    shall not by itself render the person liable to any judicial or other proceedings, but
             in any proceedings under the SFO before any court, the Handbook may be
             admissible in evidence, and if any provision set out in the Handbook appears to
             the court to be relevant to any question arising in the proceedings, it may be
             taken into account in determining the question;

      (b)    may cause the Commission to consider whether such failure adversely reflects on
             the persons fitness and properness (in so far as the relevant person is licensed
             or registered under the SFO and its obligations are stated in the Handbook);

      (c)    may cause the Commission to consider whether such failure adversely reflects on
             whether the product, the offering document and/or the advertisements should
             remain authorized;

      (d)    may cause the Commission to consider whether such failure adversely reflects on
             whether further products issued, managed and/or originated by such person,
             and/or offering documents and advertisements in relation to such products,
             should be granted authorization in the interest of the investing public (i.e. where
             there is a serious breach, the Commission may refuse to authorize new products
             issued, managed and/or originated by the person in breach and/or offering

                                                                                          Section I  1

(l)    SFO means the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Chapter 571 of the Laws of
              Hong Kong);

       (m)    SIP Code means the Code on Unlisted Structured Investment Products
              administered by the Commission as set out in Section IV of the Handbook;

       (n)    Specified Entity means a counterparty or service provider whose role and
              responsibilities with respect to a product have been specified in the applicable
              product code;

       (o)    structured investment products has the meaning ascribed to it in the SIP Code;

       (p)    unit trust(s)/mutual fund(s) means collective investment scheme(s) commonly
              regarded as unit trusts or mutual funds that are subject to the UT Code; and

       (q)    UT Code means the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds administered by the
              Commission as set out in Section II of the Handbook.

       SFCs authorization

1.8    Nothing in the Handbook shall be interpreted in a manner that alters or imposes any
       restriction upon the exercise by the Commission of any power or discretion conferred
       upon it under the SFO.

1.9    The Commission may at any time pursuant to the SFO review its authorization and may
       modify, add to or withdraw any of the conditions of such authorization, or withdraw the
       authorization, as it considers appropriate.

1.10   Where a product is described as having been authorized by the Commission, it shall be
       stated that authorization does not imply official recommendation by adding a prominent
       note in the following terms to the offering document and advertisement and other
       invitations to invest in the product:

       Note: SFC authorization is not a recommendation or endorsement of a product nor
             does it guarantee the commercial merits of a product or its performance. It does
             not mean the product is suitable for all investors nor is it an endorsement of its
             suitability for any particular investor or class of investors.

1.11   The SFC takes no responsibility for the contents of any offering documents or
       advertisements authorized by it. Product Providers are reminded that in granting
       authorization, the SFC relies on the representations made and information provided by
       the Product Provider and/or its representatives or agents in support of the authorization
       application. The making of any false or misleading representation and/or the provision of
       any false or misleading information by such person may amount to an offence under the
       SFO.

1.12   Product Providers are also reminded that SFC authorization does not imply that the SFO,
       or any other legal or regulatory requirements, have been complied with. Nothing in
       respect of an authorization may be taken as preventing the SFC from taking any action
       against any parties for breach of the SFO, or any other legal or regulatory requirements.

1.13   It is the SFCs policy intent that products offered to the public in Hong Kong are subject
       to the prior authorization of the SFC unless an exemption applies to their offering

account_source_texts.t2: Product Providers should, upon SFC’s request, obtain third party audit or verification on the management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement, record keeping of ownership and integrity of the smart contracts.
account_source_texts.t3: Product Providers should, upon SFC’s request, obtain satisfactory legal opinion to support its application.
account_source_texts.t4: Product Providers should remain and be ultimately responsible for the management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement adopted and record keeping of ownership, regardless of any outsourcing arrangement1.
account_source_texts.t5: Product Providers should ensure that proper records of token holders’ ownership interests in the product are maintained and the tokenisation arrangement is operationally compatible with service providers involved2.
account_source_texts.t6: Product Providers should have appropriate measures in place to manage and mitigate cybersecurity risks3, data privacy, system outages and recovery, and maintain a comprehensive and robust business continuity plan.
account_source_texts.t7: Product Providers should not use public-permissionless blockchain networks without additional and proper controls (eg, Product Providers to impose additional control by using a permissioned token)4.
account_source_texts.t8: 1 Given that these tokenised products are offered to the public in Hong Kong and the importance of maintaining proper records to reflect investors’ ownership, the Product Provider should remain fully responsible, despite any outsourcing arrangement such as those envisaged under 6.8 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds. For factors of consideration, please also refer to Part A of the Appendix to the Tokenised Securities Circular, where applicable, when formulating the tokenisation arrangement.
account_source_texts.t9: By adopting a see-through approach, the SFC is of the view that it is appropriate to allow primary dealing of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products, as long as the underlying product can meet all the applicable product authorisation requirements and the additional safeguards to address the new risks associated with the tokenisation arrangement (as set out in paragraphs 10-19 below).

answer.conclusion:
The preferred reading separates confirmation from request-triggered demonstration. The request qualification follows the conjunction and immediately precedes demonstration: Product Providers should confirm without awaiting a request and, upon request, demonstrate to the SFC’s satisfaction. Both verbs share all the stated objects: management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement, record keeping of ownership, and integrity of the smart contracts. Demonstration is not confined to smart-contract integrity. The satisfaction standard attaches most directly to demonstration, although a shared-standard reading remains supported.

The accompanying footnote expressly identifies the SFC as recipient of confirmation and demonstration and supplies minimum substantive content: compliance with the incorporated operational requirements and high-confidence support for the proposition that smart contracts are not subject to contract vulnerabilities or security flaws. High confidence most naturally qualifies the security proposition; attachment to the combined compliance-and-security showing is also possible. It concerns confidence in the absence of flaws, not a restriction to flaws of particularly high severity. No numerical confidence threshold, guarantee against future flaws or exhaustive evidentiary method is specified. High confidence and SFC satisfaction are distinct standards, not substitutes.

Reading the footnote as elaborating substance while preserving the main sentence’s express request condition best reconciles the two. On that reading, no request leaves confirmation expected but does not activate the specified demonstration expectation. Nevertheless, the footnote’s unqualified repetition of both verbs supports a genuine rival under which demonstration is independently expected. Extending the request condition to confirmation as well is a weaker grammatical reading. None of these readings suspends the underlying substantive responsibilities.

The neighbouring provisions concern procurement rather than the Provider’s own confirmation and demonstration. One expressly calls, upon SFC request, for third-party audit or verification covering operational soundness, ownership records and smart-contract integrity. Audit or verification are textual alternatives, not an express requirement to obtain both; that sentence does not repeat the SFC-satisfaction phrase. The other expressly calls, upon request, for a satisfactory legal opinion supporting the application. Its purpose is established, but its precise legal questions and evaluator of satisfaction are not specified. Neither form of procurement expressly substitutes for the other or for confirmation and requested demonstration. The scope of the actual request determines which expectations it activates.

Without the relevant requests, those procurement expectations are not activated by their own wording. This is not a general exemption from assessment or assurance: the supplied appendix conditionally contemplates technology and smart-contract audits and reasonable reliance on third-party audit work. Its intermediary-facing, non-exhaustive factors do not establish a universal Provider audit procedure. Providers retain ultimate responsibility despite outsourcing and should maintain proper ownership records, operational compatibility, risk controls, recovery arrangements, robust business continuity and additional proper controls when using public-permissionless networks.

These are regulatory expectations expressed using ‘should’. The extracts do not establish that the circular itself creates freestanding statutory liability. The Handbook expressly distinguishes its requirements from law and describes potential evidential, fitness-and-properness and authorisation consequences; those statements should not simply be transplanted into a definitive classification of the circular. Confirmation, document procurement, submission or authorisation does not by itself establish substantive compliance or regulatory acceptance.
unresolved: The tension between the footnote’s unqualified demonstration wording and the main sentence’s express request condition is real. Harmonisation favours preserving the condition, but does not conclusively reject independent demonstration.

The supplied wording does not conclusively settle shared attachment of SFC satisfaction or the breadth of high confidence. It specifies no precise deadline, frequency or unsolicited-submission procedure for confirmation.

The cross-referenced footnotes concerning ownership records and operational compatibility, cybersecurity, and public-permissionless networks are not delivered. The prior synthesis’s suggestion that the network-control cross-reference is substantively supplied is unsupported: the marker and main-text control expectation are present, but the referenced footnote text is not. The referenced intermediary network-risk discussion is also unverified.

The technical appendix is only partly delivered and has extraction qualifications. It supports conditional consideration of audits, resilience, interoperability, operational controls and legal issues, but not a complete audit checklist or sufficient-compliance safe harbour.

No actual request, confirmation, demonstration, assurance report, legal opinion or SFC assessment is supplied. Correspondence would establish request scope and timing; reports, methods, coverage, exceptions, remediation and operational records would distinguish procurement or submission from substantive fulfilment.
The legal-opinion wording does not identify exact legal questions, author qualifications or whose satisfaction governs. These cannot be inferred solely from the operational-assurance requirement.

Product-specific authorisation conditions, actual modifications and the circular’s precise legal consequences beyond the supplied regulatory wording remain unchecked. Those limits qualify extrapolation; merely hypothetical outside exceptions are not prerequisites to the bounded textual answer.

issues.text: The synthesis incorrectly describes absence of an SFC request as the question’s factual premise. For this assigned case, a demonstration request is stipulated. Whether external assurance or a legal opinion was also requested remains unknown. The actual correspondence would distinguish a demonstration-only request from a communication activating several expectations; separate request conditions do not require separate communications.

The detailed account repeatedly treats the incorporated footnote as unavailable, although its complete text is delivered. It expressly identifies the SFC as recipient, specifies minimum substantive content, and repeats confirmation and demonstration without an express request qualification. Its absence from a different source assignment does not make it unavailable here. The unsupported missing-footnote qualification must be removed.

The detailed account consequently omits material interpretive alternatives preserved in the synthesis. The preferred reconciliation treats the footnote as elaborating substance while retaining the main sentence’s request condition for demonstration. A genuine rival treats its unqualified demonstration wording as independently operative. Extending the request condition to confirmation is a weaker grammatical alternative. In the stipulated request case these readings do not excuse demonstration, but they differ in the no-request counterfactual.

The corrected account must retain the shared objects of confirmation and demonstration: management and operational soundness, ownership record keeping, and smart-contract integrity. SFC satisfaction most directly modifies demonstration, with a broader shared-standard reading remaining possible. The footnote adds minimum compliance with the incorporated operational requirements and high-confidence support for absence of contract vulnerabilities or security flaws. High confidence most naturally qualifies the security proposition, though broader attachment is plausible; it does not identify only high-severity flaws or replace SFC satisfaction.

Preserve the correctly stated procurement distinctions when repairing the submission. External audit or verification are alternatives addressing operational soundness, ownership records and smart-contract integrity; the procurement sentence does not expressly repeat the SFC-satisfaction standard. The separate legal opinion must be satisfactory and support the application, but its precise questions, author qualifications and evaluator are unspecified. A demonstration request alone establishes neither additional request. Procurement, submission and authorisation do not themselves establish substantive fulfilment or regulatory acceptance.

The remaining source limitations should be stated narrowly. The delivered operational provisions preserve Provider responsibility despite outsourcing and impose substantive record-keeping, compatibility, risk-management and network-control expectations independently of the disputed request attachment. Some associated explanatory footnotes and referenced intermediary material remain unverified. The supplied intermediary appendix offers conditional, non-exhaustive audit considerations, not interchangeable Provider duties or a universal safe harbour. value.conclusion: Subject to applicability and the unavailable incorporated footnote, the stronger reading of the supplied wording is that the Product Provider should confirm the listed matters independently of an SFC request and, upon request, demonstrate them to the SFC’s satisfaction. Confirmation and demonstration share the objects of management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement, ownership record keeping and smart-contract integrity. The request qualification most naturally attaches to demonstration, although a broader reading makes both acts request-dependent. The stipulated demonstration request satisfies the trigger under either reading; the practical difference concerns the no-request scenario. The satisfaction standard most directly modifies demonstration, rather than imposing a separately expressed satisfaction determination for confirmation. The demonstration request does not itself establish a request for third-party audit or verification, or for a satisfactory legal opinion supporting the application. Those requirements retain distinct request conditions, objects and standards, although one communication could expressly request several activities. Neither performance nor SFC satisfaction is established by the supplied facts.
